title: The Gurdwara Act, 1925
hook: the law passes historic gurdwaras to an elected Sikh body

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jaito, and your line was long and peaceful. Did you take one more calm step on something hard? Today, where all those long, peaceful marches led: to a law. Day nine hundred ninety.

A ballot paper, folded once, dropped into a box. It doesn't look like the end of a struggle. No march, no train on the rails, no police line. Just a voter, a list of names, and a choice. But in the story of the gurdwara reform movement, that small, dull act is the prize. For years, Sikhs had walked into beatings and arrests to answer one question: who should care for the Guru's houses? Today, the answer arrives in the plainest form there is. The Gurdwara Act.
screen: `A BALLOT IN A BOX.` → `NO MARCH, NO POLICE LINE.` → `THE ANSWER ARRIVES IN LAW.`

segments.voice: First, the question. Through the campaigns of the last weeks, at Nankana, bagh, Jaito and elsewhere, the reformers asked that historic gurdwaras be taken from hereditary mahants and returned to the sangat. Second, the law. The Sikh Gurdwaras Act was passed in Punjab. It named historic gurdwaras and placed their management under a Sikh body whose members were chosen by Sikh voters. That body soon took the name the reformers had already made famous: the SGPC. Third, what changed. Before, a shrine could pass from one mahant to his son or chosen disciple, like private property. After, those who ran it answered to an elected committee, and the committee answered to the sangat at the ballot box. That's today's line: peace won. The movement didn't take the gurdwaras by force. It kept walking until the law changed. Fourth, the root. At Ang 72 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Nanak asks how the true sangat can be known, and answers: it is where the One Name alone is praised. The reformers' claim was that a gurdwara belongs to that sangat, not to a family. The Act wrote that claim into law. It didn't settle every argument. Sikhs have debated the elected body, its politics and its choices ever since, and they still do. But a debate held through votes and committees is itself part of what was won. A voter with a ballot paper is a strange kind of hero. At the end of this story, that's exactly who the hero is.
screen: `WHO CARES FOR THE GURU'S HOUSE?` · `A LAW FOR HISTORIC GURDWARAS.` · `ANSWERING TO THE SANGAT.` · `WHERE THE ONE NAME IS PRAISED.` · then, large: `PEACE WON.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for the things you share. Sit, and let your breath slow. Bring to mind one place you hold in common with others: a gurdwara, a church, a school board, a library, a tenants' group, a town council. Something that isn't yours alone, and isn't anyone else's alone either. Breathe in, and picture the people who share it. Breathe out, and ask one quiet question: is there one way I could take part this month? If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Gurdwara, the door or house of the Guru: a law in Punjab placed historic gurdwaras under a Sikh body elected by Sikh voters, the fruit of peaceful campaigns. Today's word.
Your line: peace won. Today, vote or take part once: check your registration, attend a meeting, or volunteer for something you share with others. Day nine hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Historic gurdwaras in Punjab are managed under the Sikh Gurdwaras Act by the Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee, whose members are elected by Sikh voters; its elections and decisions are discussed and debated across the community.

notes: Please confirm: the Act passed in Punjab (by the Legislative Council), that it listed historic gurdwaras, and that it made the SGPC a statutory body elected by Sikh voters. The year is left to the title; no other dates or numbers are given.
The conditions attached to releasing Akali prisoners after the Act were contested among Sikhs; they are left out to keep one idea. Check whether a Keeper wants a line on it.
The sentence 'Sikhs have debated the elected body, its politics and its choices ever since' is meant to be neutral; check the balance.
Ang 72 paraphrased; please confirm the Ang and wording.
Original: ਗੁਰਦੁਆਰਾ, glossed as 'the door or house of the Guru'; the trapdoor avoids a root claim.

Audit: the Act created a statutory board that then adopted the SGPC's name; 'the SGPC became that body in law' simplified this, so reworded. Mahant succession was often guru-to-disciple (chela), not only father-to-son; reworded. Ang 72 is the same line used on day 961 (Amritsar Singh Sabha); kept as a block-end echo, but a Keeper may prefer another.
